# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) describes the delayed opacification of epicardial coronary arteries during angiography in the absence of significant obstructive disease. CSFP was first described by Tambe et al. in 1972, and is defined as delayed opacification of coronary vessels during angiography without any evident obstructive disease. These investigators proposed that the finding most likely reflected elevated microvascular resistance, framing the phenomenon as a cause of angina rather than a mere curiosity [2]. The condition is also referred to in the literature as cardiac syndrome Y, and coronary slow flow phenomenon is defined as the delayed opacification of the coronary vasculature at the distal level, with various hypotheses postulated about its substrate, including microvascular and endothelial dysfunction.

## Quantification

Subjective angiographic impressions were superseded by a reproducible quantitative index. Gibson and colleagues introduced the TIMI frame count, a quantitative method of assessing coronary artery flow, in Circulation in 1996. Using this method, the left anterior descending coronary artery frame counts are divided by 1.7 to correct for the longer vessel length, and a corrected TIMI frame count above 27 frames for at least one of the three major vessels defines CSFP. Subsequent work formalised CSFP using this corrected threshold [3,11].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is encountered more often than is generally appreciated. Delayed progression of contrast medium in the absence of a significant epicardial stenosis is a common angiographic finding, observed in roughly 7% of angiograms. In a large consecutive series, CSFP was identified in 5.5% of subjects referred for coronary angiography and was associated with male sex and obesity. The phenomenon is most commonly seen in young men who are smokers with metabolic syndrome, with an incidence of 1–5% in patients undergoing coronary angiography. Risk-factor studies further support this, with one cohort finding that acute coronary syndrome was the most common mode of presentation and that hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking and tobacco chewing were independent risk factors.

## Pathophysiology

Although the precise mechanism remains uncertain, several converging lines of evidence implicate the coronary microcirculation. Small-vessel dysfunction has been implicated since CSFP was first described, with investigators reporting fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial thickening and degeneration in the coronary microvessels. Histopathological studies of patients with otherwise normal epicardial arteries confirmed these microvascular abnormalities [16]. Functional studies extend these findings: Beltrame et al. indicated that CSFP was associated with a chronically elevated resting coronary microvascular tone characterized by low coronary sinus oxygen saturation as well as blunted responses to endothelial stimuli. Endothelial dysfunction is suggested by altered endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations and their response to exercise in patients with slow coronary flow. CSFP may also represent early diffuse atherosclerosis, since intravascular ultrasound studies demonstrated that patients with CSFP have diffuse intimal thickening, widespread calcification along the coronary vessel wall, and non-obstructive atheromatous coronary changes.

Inflammation appears central to the process. Most studies, along with meta-analysis, indicate that systemic inflammation plays a significant role in the development of CSF, and high-sensitivity CRP levels may indicate slowed coronary blood flow early. Platelet activation has also been implicated; mean platelet volume is increased in patients with slow coronary flow, and those presenting with unstable angina exhibit significantly increased values, suggesting altered platelet reactivity.

Notably, the equation of CSFP with microvascular dysfunction is debated. Guidelines recommend that CSFP, defined as corrected TIMI frame count >27, can diagnose coronary microvascular dysfunction, and CSFP has historically been regarded as a sign of coronary endothelial dysfunction. However, more recent invasive physiology data suggest the relationship is imperfect, since the corrected TIMI frame count had only a weak negative correlation with basal average peak velocity and a weak positive correlation with basal microvascular resistance.

## Clinical presentation and prognosis

CSFP is clinically meaningful. It is a frequent finding typically observed in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes, and although well known for approximately four decades the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear, with over 80% of patients experiencing recurrent chest pain. The condition is not entirely benign: CSFP usually has a benign long-term outcome but may be associated with relapses, and occasional ventricular arrhythmias and even sudden cardiac death have been reported. An electrophysiological substrate is suggested by the finding that QTc dispersion, indicating increased risk for ventricular arrhythmias and cardiovascular mortality, was significantly higher in patients with slow coronary artery flow. Case reports document CSFP with normalization of flow after intracoronary adenosine in patients with nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and increased QTc dispersion.

## Management

No definitive treatment guideline exists, but several agents have shown benefit. Vasodilators such as dipyridamole and adenosine, which affect the microvessels, improve coronary flow in CSFP patients, whereas agents targeting larger epicardial arteries such as glyceryl trinitrate have failed to normalize coronary flow. Calcium channel blockade has the strongest evidence: in a randomised crossover study, mibefradil significantly reduced total angina frequency by 56%, prolonged episodes of angina by 74%, and sublingual nitrate consumption by 59%, and improved physical quality of life. Beta-blockade with vasodilatory properties may help, as nebivolol improves endothelial function, controls chest pain, decreases C-reactive protein, and significantly improves coronary flow. Oral dipyridamole has likewise been used successfully [19], and standard antianginal combinations may improve symptoms and quality of life [18].

## Conclusion

CSFP is a relatively common angiographic finding linked to elevated microvascular resistance, endothelial dysfunction, low-grade inflammation and diffuse early atherosclerosis. While often regarded as benign, it causes recurrent disabling angina and carries a small risk of arrhythmia. CSFP should be situated within the broader framework of coronary microvascular disease defined by the COVADIS group [27], although the precise relationship between angiographic slow flow and invasively measured microvascular dysfunction warrants ongoing study.
